**Ecology** — how organisms interact with each other and their environment — symbiosis and host–microbe partnerships, competition, herbivory and trophic interactions, community structure, resilience and regime shifts in ecosystems (ADR-028). How a partner comes to live inside another and depend on it is endosymbiosis (ADR-055).

| [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | Goulet, Erill, Ascunce, Finley & Javan (2020), Frontiers in Physiology 11:566968, a review. A coral is a consortium: the animal plus the Symbiodiniaceae, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses in its body, mucus and skeleton, and neighbours are excluded by definition. Membership can change, so one colony may be a different holobiont at different times. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. Whether the holobiont is the unit of selection is asked, not answered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md)); worth reading as a short, explicit statement of why a coral should be studied as a composite of host and microbes rather than as an animal with passengers. It is a mini-review with no data of its own (about 3,700 words), and its strongest point is conceptual: traits such as thermal tolerance belong to host–symbiont combinations, not to either partner. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. It poses, and does not answer, whether the coral holobiont is a unit of selection. |
| [LIT-711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-711.md) | Phase Shifts, Herbivory, and the Resilience of Coral Reefs to Climate Change | Hughes et al. (2007), Current Biology 17(4):360–365. A replicated fish-exclusion experiment at Orpheus Island, Great Barrier Reef, begun in 2000 after the 1998 mass bleaching: four roofless 5 × 5 m cages, four partial cages and four open plots, over 30 months. Excluding large and medium fishes produced a phase shift to Sargassum-dominated macroalgae. Coral recovery was suppressed, through about two-thirds lower recruitment and more than double the mortality of surviving colonies. In the controls, coral cover nearly doubled to 20%, mainly by recruitment of taxa that bleaching had removed locally. Reopened cages lost their macroalgae within 30 days. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-558.md)), main text and methods; the supplement was out of reach. Worth reading as the controlled experiment behind the claim that reef recovery after bleaching depends on an ecological interaction, not only on surviving corals. On an inshore Great Barrier Reef crest after the 1998 bleaching, roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of four 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae rose to a mean of 56% cover in the cages against 4.1% and 1.7% in partial cages and open plots. Coral cover in the cages rose only from 6.0% to 7.7%, against 19.2% and 20.2%, because recruitment was about two-thirds lower and mortality of established colonies more than double. It is one site with four replicates per treatment. The cages excluded all large and medium fishes, not herbivores alone, and the macroalgal state vanished within 30 days of reopening them. |
| [LIT-712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-712.md) | Defining Coral Bleaching as a Microbial Dysbiosis within the Coral Holobiont | Boilard, Dubé, Gruet, Mercière, Hernandez-Agreda & Derome (2020), Microorganisms 8(11):1682, a review. Bleaching, the breakdown of the coral–dinoflagellate symbiosis, is redefined as a succession of three holobiont dysbiosis stages: (i) the microbiota buffers the stress and keeps essential functions; (ii) the algal partners are reorganised by shuffling or switching, with or without transient bleaching; (iii) the stress exceeds both buffers, symbionts are lost for good, opportunists invade and the coral dies, and at reef scale algae take over. The stages are a proposal, with no criteria to tell them apart, and the authors concede that microbial shifts are not shown to cause bleaching. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-556](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-556.md)); worth reading as the statement of the "adaptive dysbiosis" account of coral bleaching, which treats bleaching as three successive holobiont states: microbial buffering, reorganisation of the algal partners by shuffling or switching, and an irreversible breakdown ending in death. It is a review with no data of its own, and the account is a proposal. Its own text says that bacterial shifts during bleaching cannot yet be read as cause or consequence, so the title's "microbial dysbiosis" claims more than the body supports. |

| [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md) | Catastrophic regime shifts in ecosystems: linking theory to observation | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), Trends in Ecology & Evolution 18:648–656. A regime shift can come from a bifurcation, not only a large shock. Field data give hints that are never conclusive. Experiments can demonstrate alternative attractors: initial states fixing end states, a temporary disturbance causing a lasting shift, or hysteresis. Positive feedbacks must be strong enough. Slow return can mimic a new state, as when a biomanipulated lake stayed clear for six years and then slipped back. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-571.md)): in full, from a UC Berkeley course page. Worth reading for its standard of evidence for alternative stable states. Field patterns (jumps in time series, multimodal distributions, dual relationships to a driver) are only hints. Experiments are what demonstrate: different initial states lead to different end states, a temporary disturbance causes a lasting shift, or the response to forward and backward change shows hysteresis. Positive feedback is not enough unless strong. Long return times can mimic an alternative state. |
| [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md) | Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems | Holling (1973), Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 4:1–23. Stability is how quickly and smoothly a system returns to equilibrium after a disturbance. Resilience is its ability to absorb change in state variables, drivers and parameters and still persist, a matter of the size of its domain of attraction. A system can be highly resilient and unstable, as the spruce budworm forest is. Managing for a stable maximum yield can shrink resilience until a rare event flips the system. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-572](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-572.md)): in full, from IIASA's authorised reprint. Worth reading as the origin of the distinction between stability and resilience. Stability is the speed and smoothness of return to an equilibrium after a disturbance. Resilience is the capacity to absorb change and still persist, measured by the size of the domain of attraction and how near its boundary the system sits. The two can trade off: management for constancy can erode resilience. Evidence is a set of case histories (lakes, spruce budworm, salmon, fire), not tests. |

| [LIT-1824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1824.md) v2 | Tractable models of ecological assembly | Serván & Allesina (2021), Ecology Letters 24: 1029–1037. Represents assembly by rare, low-density, well-separated invasions as a directed graph on feasible sub-communities, and proves that sequential (bottom-up) and all-at-once (top-down) assembly reach the same end-points when the graph is acyclic and attractors are exactly the uninvadable sub-communities. For competitive Lotka–Volterra with A = D(v)BD(w), B symmetric with positive entries, MacArthur's Lyapunov function orders the sub-communities, so both hold: with B positive definite there is one end-point, the sub-community of greatest total biomass when r = v, reachable by invasions without extinctions; with B indefinite there are several, and order of arrival matters. Read it knowing that the copy read is the dissertation chapter of August 2020, not the Ecology Letters version, which was not compared; that order-independence (a single end-point) needs the interaction matrix positive definite, and an indefinite one still has priority effects; and that the step from the Lyapunov function to acyclicity is asserted, not written out. |

Neither carries this paper's methods, intervals or sample sizes, and the per-generation figure differs between this abstract (about 40%) and the 2008 review (about 30%, or 30–40%) without being reconciled in anything read. |
| [LIT-2163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2163.md) | Factors affecting success of conservation translocations of terrestrial vertebrates: A global systematic review | Morris, Brook, Moseby & Johnson (2021), read as the 2021 preprint. A global database of 514 conservation translocations of terrestrial vertebrates (1895–2017), from Web of Science and the IUCN's "Global re-introduction perspectives" reports, modelled on two outcomes: categorical success calibrated to practitioners' own labels (n = 257) and generation-weighted population growth (n = 87). Success rises with numbers released up to about 20–50 individuals, then plateaus; Oceania does worse. Captive-bred and wild stock have similar reported success ("wild 70.2%, captive 76.0%"), but captive-bred stock has negative mean growth (−2.8 against +2.2) and captive sourcing is among the strongest predictors of growth; soft and hard release have similar reported success (79.8% against 75.0%), but hard release shows higher growth (+5.6 against −1.3). The authors read the captive gap as possible leniency "with success criteria" among practitioners invested in captive breeding. The outcome scale's top rung is a population "likely to persist without further augmentation", which only 24.8% of the IUCN successes reached. Raw group means with wide spreads, not adjusted contrasts. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1657](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1657.md)) as the authors' EcoEvoRxiv preprint, "Lessons from a century of conservation translocations" (doi:10.32942/osf.io/hnzqk, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), not the published version, which could not be reached; any change between the two is unknown. Worth reading as the largest standardized global synthesis of terrestrial-vertebrate translocations (514, 1895–2017) and for showing that practitioner-judged success and population growth after release disagree: captive-bred stock and soft release match wild stock and hard release on reported success but show lower population growth. Its limits: source and release method are raw group means with large spreads in a growth subset of 87, not model-adjusted contrasts; success is self-reported and calibrated on a handful of questionnaire returns; reporting bias is strong (8% failures in the IUCN reports); the supplement and the coefficients' figures were not seen. |
| [LIT-2165](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2165.md) | Merging community assembly into the regime-shift approach for informing ecological restoration | Kadowaki, Nishijima, Kéfi, Kameda & Sasaki (2018). Alternative stable states have been studied by community assembly (species composition, competition, priority effects, small scales) and by regime shifts (aggregate state, feedbacks through the abiotic environment, large scales); the authors argue restoration needs both. A two-species Lotka–Volterra model with environmental mortality and facilitation shows hysteresis in total abundance, composition changing before the collapse that total abundance hides, and restoration that succeeds or fails by which species is reintroduced first. Three cases illustrate that restoring conditions can fail against the degraded state's own legacy: a fire-suppressed wetland, Japanese lakes after eutrophication, and Yellowstone after wolves were reintroduced. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1677](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1677.md)) from the publisher's version on HAL Montpellier (hal-01938760, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); worth reading as a restoration review that says why removing a pressure can fail to restore a system with alternative states: the degraded phase leaves a reinforcing legacy of its own (hardwoods that stop fire spreading, organic sludge that favours a floating competitor, eroded beaver sites), so recovery needs biotic manipulation, by removal or by reintroduction in the right order, as well as restored conditions. A perspective with a toy model the authors call "not novel" and three narrative cases drawn from other studies; no effect sizes, no test of bistability in any case, and no case followed after the intervention stopped. Registered as a stand-in for Suding, Gross & Houseman (2004), [LIT-2169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2169.md), for its framing only. |
| [LIT-2167](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2167.md) | Direct experimental evidence for alternative stable states: a review | Schröder, Persson & De Roos (2005). A review of the manipulation experiments that test for alternative stable states by four routes: discontinuity in response to a driver, non-recovery after a perturbation, divergence from different initial conditions, and random divergence. A state counts as stable only if it outlasts one turnover of its longest-lived organisms. Of 35 experiments, 14 fail that bar or another requirement; of the 21 conclusive, 13 show alternative states and 8 their absence. Bistability was found in 10 of 12 conclusive laboratory experiments and 3 of 9 field experiments, none in marine habitats or whole ecosystems; of 15 non-recovery tests, 3 were positive. Abrupt shifts, bimodality and feedback alone do not show alternative states. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1666](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1666.md)), body in full, from the third author's University of Amsterdam staff page; worth reading as the direct-evidence test for alternative stable states: of 35 manipulation experiments, 21 were conclusive over at least one turnover of the longest-lived organisms, 13 showing alternative states and 8 their absence; positives came mostly from laboratory systems (10 of 12) against field systems (3 of 9), and only 3 of 15 tests of non-recovery after a pressure was removed were positive, all in terrestrial grazing systems. Its limits: the search ends in 2004, turnover times are approximate, the classification is the authors' judgement, and the appendix table extracted garbled, so nothing drawn from it is verified here. |
| [LIT-2169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2169.md) v2 | Alternative states and positive feedbacks in restoration ecology | Suding, Gross & Houseman (2004), a short TREE review with no data of its own, read in full in [NOTE-1700](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1700.md). Restoration has assumed "that, once the historical physical environment is re-established, natural successional processes will return the biotic system to its original condition"; that holds where degradation altered only the environment, and fails where the degraded state has built feedbacks of its own: invader-driven nitrogen and fire cycles, herbivory on regenerating plants, lost seed sources, or bare soil where "less vegetation holds less water". Restoration must then disrupt the feedback or move the state directly, often by several actions together ("burning and adding native seeds"), as when transplanted plugs of a former dominant restore a salt marsh that reducing herbivory did not. The review ends in a separate maintenance phase, not in withdrawal, and concedes that rigorous tests of alternative stable states "are beyond the scope of most restoration efforts". Here as the ecological form of [CLAIM-463](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-463.md) and support in kind for [CLAIM-604](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-604.md); it does not meet [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md)'s bar, and says so. | Active — read 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1700](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1700.md)) from the typeset.io copy of the publisher's typeset version (https://typeset.io/pdf/alternative-states-and-positive-feedbacks-in-restoration-3p92oa7stw.pdf, which redirects to the same path on scispace.com, typeset.io's current name), 8 pages, checked to be the work by title, authors, running heads, pages 46–53 and the printed DOI. Worth reading as the standard statement that restoring a degraded system's historical conditions or disturbance regime need not restore its community, because the degraded state is held by biotic–abiotic feedbacks that restoration must break first, with a four-constraint typology, a three-case scheme (Fig. 2) and a six-step practice cycle (Fig. 3) that ends in maintenance. Its limits: a review with no data of its own; every effect size is second-hand, from single cited studies with no designs or sample sizes; and no case measures what happens when the intervention is withdrawn after a state shift. The authors concede that rigorous tests of alternative stable states are beyond most restoration efforts. |
| [LIT-2172](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2172.md) | A call for practical spatially patterned forest restoration methods | Holl, Reid, Zahawi, de Siqueira & Brancalion (2024). An opinion article on applied nucleation, planting patches of trees to speed forest recovery, and other spatially patterned methods. Nuclei work by "attracting seed dispersing animals", improving conditions for seedlings within and at their edges, and spreading; perches and bat boxes "do not improve local conditions for seedling establishment and growth" and soon decay, whereas "once established, trees attract dispersers and modify microsite conditions continuously". Spread "may be slow and highly unpredictable" and is seldom measured. A nucleus of about 64 m² is cited as the minimum in tropical moist forest; planting 1–5% of a site is judged too little. Nuclei cost more than strips where planting is mechanized and less on steep, hand-planted ground. The method does not fit where dispersers are gone or regeneration is invasive. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1676](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1676.md)) from the publisher's version deposited in the NSF Public Access Repository; worth reading as the senior author's own account, twelve years on, of what applied nucleation does and where it fails, and as the stand-in for the unread Corbin & Holl (2012), [LIT-2179](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2179.md), on mechanism, comparisons, cost and nucleus size. It separates planted trees, which once established keep drawing dispersers and improving microsites, from perches and bat boxes, which leave no improved conditions and decay within years, and insists that nuclei must also spread, which is slow and rarely measured. A five-page opinion article: its 64 m² minimum and 1–5% planted share are cited from others or unpublished, its cost comparison is unpublished, and it reports nothing on what follows the end of maintenance. |
| [LIT-2173](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2173.md) | What is better for animal conservation translocation programmes: Soft- or hard-release? A phylogenetic meta-analytical approach | Resende, Viana-Junior, Young & Azevedo (2021), unread beyond the Crossref abstract. From that abstract, unverified until read: a phylogenetic meta-analysis of 61 effect sizes from 17 studies of 17 species finds soft release "approximate 40% better than the hard-release protocol (Estimates = 0.44, CI 95: 0.11–0.76)", an advantage "driven mostly by terrestrial reptile translocations"; for birds and mammals, and on success metrics other than movement, the two release techniques had similar effects, and whether animals were captive or wild in origin did not change the comparison. Here because it is the controlled-comparison counterpart to Morris et al. (2021), [LIT-2163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2163.md), whose global review found no benefit of soft release on reported success and lower population growth after it, and because soft release (pens, supplemental food at the release site) is transient support whose removal is the record's question ([CLAIM-597](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-597.md), [QUESTION-398](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-398.md)). | Unavailable — no lawful full text reached on 2026-11-05; only the Crossref abstract was read. Looked at: the green copy at salford-repository.worktribe.com, a Cloudflare "Just a moment" check (403); usir.salford.ac.uk, which redirects to the same host; and CORE's API, which returned a Cloudflare redirect page. No host was retried past its block. The publisher's page was not tried. |
| [LIT-2176](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2176.md) v2 | The fitness consequences of wildlife conservation translocations: a meta-analysis | Gross, Wilson & Wolak (2023), unread beyond the Crossref abstract. From that abstract, unverified until read: across 821 comparisons from 171 studies of 101 species, translocated organisms "have 64% decreased odds of out‐performing their wild‐resident counterparts"; "Pre‐release animal enrichment significantly reduced performance disparities"; and there was no overall effect of captive generation time. Here because it measures the gap between animals that were moved, often after captive support, and those that never needed it, and names one pre-release support, enrichment, that narrowed the gap: the distinction between support that replaces capacity and support that builds it that [CLAIM-602](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-602.md) and [QUESTION-398](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-398.md) put. Its finding on captive stock agrees in direction with Morris et al. (2021), [LIT-2163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2163.md). | Unfetched — searched 2026-11-05 for a lawful full text; one exists but this client could not fetch it, so it is not read (ADR-053); only the Crossref abstract was read. The bioRxiv preprint, the authors' manuscript, doi:10.1101/2023.01.14.524021 (v1 2023-01-17, v2 2023-06-12, CC BY-NC-ND), was blocked at biorxiv.org by a Cloudflare 1015 rate limit on 2026-11-05. Also looked at: the Auburn ETD hosts etd.auburn.edu and holocron.lib.auburn.edu, both failing TLS verification, not overridden; and Europe PMC, which has no full text. No host was retried past its block. The publisher's page was not tried. Whether the preprint differs from the published paper is unverified. A browser fetch of the bioRxiv preprint is the cheapest way to read it. It stays Unfetched until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-2177](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2177.md) | Active restoration increases tree species richness and recruitment of large-seeded taxa after 16–18 years | Schubert, Zahawi, Oviedo-Brenes, Rosales & Holl (2024). In ten southern Costa Rican pasture sites, plots were left to natural regeneration, planted with six tree islands (86 trees per 0.25 ha) or fully planted (313), and all were cleared by machete every three months "for the first 2.5 years", then left. At 16–18 years both planted treatments had more later-successional seedlings and saplings and less variable composition than natural regeneration, with plantation matching reference forest in large-seeded recruits and nucleation intermediate. Yet "Trees (≥5 cm dbh) in all restoration treatments continued to be dominated by a few early-successional species and originally transplanted individuals", and the planted species' seedlings seldom reached the sapling layer. Natural regeneration progressed but was variable and risked stalling; recovery leaned on the region's abundant remnant seed sources. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1660](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1660.md)) from the publisher's version of record deposited in the NSF Public Access Repository, all but the reference list and Appendix S1; worth reading as a clean case of support withdrawn early whose effects were measured long after, and as the stand-in for the unread Holl et al. (2020), [LIT-2145](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2145.md), on the experiment's long-term recruitment. Weeding stopped at 2.5 years; at 16–18 years both planted treatments still had richer later-successional recruitment and more predictable composition than natural regeneration, yet in every treatment the tree layer was still pioneers and the planted cohort, whose own seedlings seldom reached the sapling layer. Eight or nine plots per treatment in one seed-rich region, with only four planted species, island sizes not analysed apart, and no cost data. |
| [LIT-2179](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2179.md) v2 | Applied nucleation as a forest restoration strategy | Corbin & Holl (2012), unread. A review of applied nucleation, planting patches of trees so that they draw seed dispersers and improve microsites, and spread, as a forest restoration strategy, set against full plantation and natural regeneration. From the works that stand in for it and cite it, and unverified until read: it is cited as the source of the current use of the term, for "patches of vegetation" that "are actively seeded or planted to accelerate forest recovery", for the open question of strips against nuclei, and for the claim that nucleation lowers project costs. Here because a nucleus is support meant to be withdrawn once the forest carries on by itself, the question [CLAIM-597](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-597.md) and [QUESTION-399](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-399.md) put. | Unfetched — searched 2026-11-05 for a lawful full text; one exists but this client could not fetch it, so it is not read (ADR-053). Two free copies were found by web search: the eScholarship copy, escholarship.org/uc/item/0t0109x6, and the CORE copy, core.ac.uk/download/357583679.pdf. Neither was tried, because on 2026-11-05 both hosts had already answered this session with bot checks: an AWS WAF challenge on escholarship.org (HTTP 202, for another item) and a Cloudflare challenge on api.core.ac.uk. Also looked at: Crossref (licence Elsevier TDM only, not open access); OpenAlex (oa_status closed, no repository full text) and Semantic Scholar (open-access PDF closed); the Yale ELTI resource page, which gives metadata and links only; old.ser-rrc.org, refused by the agent proxy; and the NSF Public Access Repository, which does not hold it. No UCSC lab publications page was found; ResearchGate was not tried. Two later works by its senior author's group stand in, read: Holl, Reid, Zahawi, de Siqueira & Brancalion (2024), LIT-2172, for the mechanism of applied nucleation, its comparison with plantation and natural regeneration, its cost and minimum nucleus size, as the authors now hold them; and Schubert et al. (2024), LIT-2177, for the long-term results of the Costa Rican experiment. Neither stands in for this review's own literature tables or wording. A browser fetch of the eScholarship copy is the cheapest way to read it. It stays Unfetched until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-2183](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2183.md) | Genetic rescue, the greater prairie chicken and the problem of conservation reliance in the Anthropocene | Mussmann et al. (2017). Translocations of greater prairie chickens into Illinois in 1992–1998 made the population a textbook case of genetic rescue. Twenty years on, 1831 shed feathers from six leks, genotyped at 21 microsatellites, show small, declining, bottlenecked and inbred populations, with heterozygosity unchanged across pre- and post-translocation samples. The authors read the earlier rise as demographic, not genetic, rescue, and argue that translocation without restored habitat, in their words, may "invoke long-term intensive management (i.e. the perpetuation of conservation reliance)": two factors set the baseline of reliance, extrinsic threat and intrinsic small-population limits, "and both must be alleviated in tandem". | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1670](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1670.md)) from the open copy in PubMed Central (PMC5367285, CC BY 4.0); worth reading as a case of supplied individuals, translocated greater prairie chickens, whose benefit to an Illinois population was by the authors' account "ambiguous or transitory", with a conceptual model in which reliance on management can fall below a threshold only if extrinsic threat and intrinsic small-population limits are relieved together. Also one of three neighbours standing in for the unread Scott et al. (2010), [LIT-2146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2146.md), for the concept of conservation reliance only; its 84 % figure and definition are cited to Goble et al. (2012), unread. One species in two counties, four years of feather genotypes, a pre-translocation baseline of 32 birds over 19 years that the authors call equivocal, and a threshold that is drawn, not measured. |
| [LIT-2185](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2185.md) | Genetic adaptation to captivity can occur in a single generation | Christie, Marine, French & Blouin (2012). A pedigree of 12,700 Hood River winter steelhead at eight microsatellite loci over 15 run-years tests two predictions that domestication selection makes and relaxed selection does not. Both hold. First-generation hatchery fish "had nearly double the lifetime reproductive success" of wild fish when both were spawned in the hatchery; and among wild broodstock, those most successful in the hatchery left offspring least successful in the wild (0.62 against 2.05 returning offspring), in 7 of 8 run-years. Inbreeding cannot explain it. The one exception, a release year with few broodstock, few smolts reared at low density and released larger, "points to crowding as a possible selection pressure". The authors conclude that less than one generation in captivity can produce "a rapid, genetically based fitness reduction in the wild". | Active — main text read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1652](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1652.md)) from the free full text on PMC (PMC3252900); the supplementary tables were not read. Worth reading as the test that settled the mechanism of the fitness loss Araki, Cooper & Blouin (2007), [LIT-2159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2159.md), measured in the same Hood River steelhead: adaptation to captivity, shown by a hatchery advantage of hatchery-born fish and a tradeoff between broodstock success in the hatchery and their offspring's in the wild, within one generation. One population; the hatchery-advantage test is significant only with one run-year excluded; the traits selected are not identified. |
| [LIT-2192](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2192.md) | Fitness of hatchery-reared salmonids in the wild | Araki, Berejikian, Ford & Blouin (2008). A review of studies comparing hatchery and wild salmonids' fitness in the same natural habitat, with a quantitative-genetic model. Hatchery fish are generally less fit in the wild; nonlocal stocks kept closed for 5–10 generations worst (lifetime relative fitness 0.02–0.37); stocks from local wild broodstock "generally perform better than nonlocal stocks, but often worse than wild fish". For the authors' Hood River steelhead the decline is fast, inherited and cumulative from the first to the second hatchery generation. Of relaxed selection, inbreeding and domestication selection, the last is judged "The last and most likely explanation", and the model finds that it can give a decline of more than 30% per generation on one trait only under strong selection in both settings and high heritability, plausibly on several traits. Using local wild broodstock mitigates the loss "to some extent", and no rise in wild productivity from hatcheries is documented. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1668.md)) from the open-access Europe PMC full text of PMC3352433; worth reading as the same laboratory's review of hatchery against wild salmonid fitness in the wild, the stand-in for its Science paper of 2007 ([LIT-2159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2159.md)), whose relative-fitness estimates and design it reports, and for its model of when domestication selection can account for a loss of more than 30% per hatchery generation. Fourteen studies, mostly steelhead, with little power below a 10–15% difference; the model is one generation and, in its worked form, one trait; the mechanism is argued, not measured. |
